title: P2P-IPC pinned-page starvation and alloc coalesce notes
content:
Summary:

Field notes from a set of investigations into reproducible OOMs during mixed-workload serving on multi-GPU nodes. This focuses on a cross-cutting root cause we observed: pinned host page exhaustion and suboptimal allocator coalescing when CUDA IPC / peer-to-peer transfers are involved, leading to persistent small-free-run fragmentation and cudaMalloc retries.

Context / why this mattered:
- Symptoms: intermittent 500/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED errors from workers serving long-chat sequences + bursty embedding requests. OOMs appear even when total resident RSS and GPU utilization are moderate.
- Repro window: higher probability under mixed-precision quantized payloads (4-bit packing) and when we do cross-GPU KV-cache shuffles (P2P memcpy via CUDA IPC handles).

High-level hypothesis chain (initial):
1) CUDA IPC creates pinned host staging buffers (or pins pages when mapping remote GPU memory) which are accounted separately from normal device heap and sometimes pinned pages are not returned promptly to the host pinned pool.
2) Our internal tensor allocator (hybrid slab + arena) emits many small allocations for quantized tensors and per-request scratch. These small allocations become interleaved with the pinned-mapped regions, preventing coalescing of adjacent free spans in device arena.
3) The device allocator's freelist coalescing heuristic only coalesces contiguous device blocks if they are released within the same stream epoch; IPC-backed ranges or remote-mapped ranges break that contiguity logic, creating many small unusable holes.
4) Over time (minutes to hours), the largest contiguous free block size shrinks below a threshold required by certain kernel workspaces, triggering cudaMalloc fallback/retry loops and eventual OOM.

Telemetry pulled / signals looked at:
- heap_free_bytes and largest_free_block_bytes per GPU (we added a probe). Observed largest_free_block_bytes decay from ~28GB -> 1.2GB across ~6 hours on the problematic nodes while total_free_bytes only fell from 32GB -> 28GB.
- cudaMalloc retry count spikes correlated to periods of heavy cross-GPU cache syncs.
- pinned_host_pages_in_use (host-side pinned page pool) rose steadily during repro runs and did not drop after the task completed for ~20s.
- nvlink activity / P2P memcpy rate high during bursts.
- trace of stream events shows device free events occurring, but coalesce step failing due to a 'mapped' flag on adjacent blocks.

Reproduction steps (minimal):
1) Start a two-GPU node (A/B) with default platform allocator and our latest runtime build (with IPC enabled in inter-GPU routing).
2) Spawn 200 concurrent small-chunk embedding requests on GPU A (quantized 4-bit tensors). Each request: allocate ~10–50 small tensors and a 4MB scratch workspace, then free.
3) Every 500ms, perform a KV-cache sync from GPU A -> GPU B via CUDA IPC cuMemcpyPeerAsync of pinned-mapped handles (simulate our checkpointing/replication path).
4) Run for 2 hours. Observe pinned_host_pages_in_use and largest_free_block_bytes.

Observed experimental results (summary):
- With IPC enabled: after ~40–90 minutes the largest contiguous free block drops below 2GB and kernel workspace allocation for long-context attention kernels starts to fail, causing fallbacks that increase latency and eventually OOM on one of the GPUs.
- With IPC disabled (fallback to host copy via staging buffer with explicit cudaHostAlloc/cudaMemcpy): fragmentation still increases but at a slower rate; pinned pages are still allocated but are freed faster.
- With a modified allocator that forces eager coalescing irrespective of "foreign_mapped" metadata: fragmentation growth slowed, but we saw correctness risks when remote-mapped ranges were used concurrently (races).
- Introducing a short delay between release of mapped blocks and reuse (cool-down) reduced observable coalescing bugs but cost latency.

Detailed root-cause analysis (technical):
- The allocator uses per-stream free queues. When a block is freed, it is appended to a stream's retired list with a retire_epoch counter. Coalescing only happens when an epoch boundary is reached and adjacent blocks are not marked mapped/foreign. CUDA IPC mapped ranges set a flag (we mark them as "foreign_mapped") so that our coalescer avoids merging to prevent accidental freeing of memory still referenced by another process. However, in our usage pattern the remote references are transient and the IPC unmap path sometimes races with the coalescer. The safe-but-conservative behavior leaves many tiny holes.
- Additionally, pinned pages on the host used by IPC get registered and deregistered through the driver asynchronously; our monitoring shows driver unregister operations delayed by 10–30s under heavy P2P traffic, prolonging the time a region remains 'mapped' and further interfering with device coalescing.
- Finally, our small-allocation size classes (32,64,128,256B) create internal fragmentation when requests fall between sizes and we align to 256B due to kernel alignment constraints; these alignment paddings, when repeated, form usable but not coalescible regions.

Why this looks like OOM despite room overall:
- Kernel workspace requests (attention and kv-cache rehydrate) ask for large contiguous device ranges (>2GB). When largest_free_block_bytes < required workspace size, allocation fails even though cumulative free bytes are sufficient. This then triggers fallback slow paths that allocate on host or recompile smaller-chunk kernels — both increase memory churn and push the system into true OOM.

Mitigation options (short-term & long-term):
Short-term (low friction):
- Add a periodic background coalescer that is IPC-aware: wait a short grace period after IPC unmap events before rejecting mapped merging — this reduces holes without introducing races. (Complexity: moderate; tradeoff between correctness and reclaim speed).
- Throttle concurrent IPC map/unmap frequency from the replication path: batch KV-cache syncs to reduce map churn. (Simple, effective).
- Increase default reservation ratio for large contiguous workspace reservations (raise lazy-reserve threshold) so that critical kernels can draw from reserved slabs rather than relying on largest_free_block. (Palliative).

Medium-term (engineering effort):
- Implement robust reference-counting for IPC-mapped ranges in the allocator (cross-process handle reference tracking). When driver unmap completes, decrement and allow coalescing immediately. Requires integration with our IPC lifecycle and careful testing.
- Improve small-allocation packing: introduce compacting bins that pack many tiny allocations into a single slab that can be freed/coalesced in bulk (reduces header overhead and alignment waste).
- Provide an allocator-mode flag (production mode) that prefers pre-reservation for long-context workloads and disables aggressive small-chunk placements near reservation slabs.

Long-term (research/architectural):
- Explore kernel-level pinned-page metrics and driver patches with NVIDIA to reduce unmap latency under nvlink/P2P hotspots.
- Consider moving to a hybrid model where large contiguous workspaces are served from a separate pool with different lifetime semantics (pool per long-context model) so the general-purpose allocator doesn't have to satisfy both tiny-slab churn and huge contiguous allocations.

Immediate action items (owner / ETA):
- [Ravi] Throttle KV-cache sync batching (config flag) — experimental rollout by 2024-11-20.
- [Marcus] Add probe for driver unmap latency and surface metric pinned_unmap_latency_ms — 2024-11-10 (done, initial metrics in graphite).
- [Amelia] Implement short-grace periodic coalescer (pooled task runs every 5s) and test on staging — prototype by 2024-12-01.
- [Eng-team] Write regression test that simulates IPC churn and verifies largest_free_block_bytes not degrade under sustained load — 2025-01-15.

Notes / open questions:
- Are there edge cases where remote process genuinely holds onto the mapping for >30s? We need to audit the IPC lifetime in the replication worker.
- Should we add an application-level flag to disable IPC for customers who prefer deterministic allocator behavior (making it a supported config)?
- Could the driver unmap latency be caused by pinned host page exhaustion on the node (system-wide) and not strictly by our process? Need cross-team SRE telemetry (host pinned page pool usage).

Appendix: quick trace snippet (simplified):
- t=00:10:12: cudaMalloc 4MB -> success (largest_free=28GB)
- t=00:10:13: many small frees from stream-7 -> they go to retired list with epoch=103
- t=00:10:13: ipc_map(remote_handle) -> mark device block @0x7fa... as foreign_mapped
- t=00:10:14: epoch++ -> coalescer scans but sees foreign_mapped and skips merge
- t=00:10:42: driver unmap event for same block (observed delay)
- t=00:10:42..00:11:02: coalescer runs but we required a fresh retire event to coalesce (race) -> blocks remain separate

Closing thought: the problem is compounded because IPC semantics and driver behavior inject asynchrony into our allocation lifecycle. Conservative allocator invariants make us safe but brittle under sustained P2P churn. A combination of batching maps/unmaps, a short-grace IPC-aware coalescer, and targeted reservation for large workspaces should materially reduce the observed OOMs with modest engineering cost.

If anyone wants the raw traces / nvprof captures used in these notes I have them on gcs: gs://redwood-internal/alloc-investigations/p2p-ipc-2024-11/*.tgz
